entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11808"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 40</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.49">Eze 40:1-49</reference>. The Remaining Chapters, the Fortieth through Forty-eighth, Give an Ideal Picture of the Restored Jewish Temple.</title> <div sID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> The arrangements as to the land and the temple are, in many particulars, different from those subsisting before the captivity. There are things in it so improbable physically as to preclude a purely literal interpretation. The general truth seems to hold good that, as Israel served the nations for his rejection of Messiah, so shall they serve him in the person of Messiah, when he shall acknowledge Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.12">Is 60:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.17-Zech.14.19">Zec 14:17-19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">Psa 72:11</reference>). The ideal temple exhibits, under Old Testament forms (used as being those then familiar to the men whom Ezekiel, a priest himself, and one who delighted in sacrificial images, addresses), not the precise literal outline, but the essential character of the worship of Messiah as it shall be when He shall exercise sway in Jerusalem among His own people, the Jews, and thence to the ends of the earth. The very fact that the whole is a vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference>), not an oral face-to-face communication such as that granted to Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6-Num.12.8">Nu 12:6-8</reference>), implies that the directions are not to be understood so precisely literally as those given to the Jewish lawgiver. The description involves things which, taken literally, almost involve natural impossibilities. The square of the temple, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.20">Eze 42:20</reference>, is six times as large as the circuit of the wall enclosing the old temple, and larger than all the earthly Jerusalem. Ezekiel gives three and a half miles and one hundred forty yards to his temple square. The boundaries of the ancient city were about two and a half miles. Again, the city in Ezekiel has an area between three or four thousand square miles, including the holy ground set apart for the prince, priests, and Levites. This is nearly as large as the whole of Judea west of the Jordan. As Zion lay in the center of the ideal city, the one-half of the sacred portion extended to nearly thirty miles south of Jerusalem, that is, covered nearly the whole southern territory, which reached only to the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.19">Eze 47:19</reference>), and yet five tribes were to have their inheritance on that side of Jerusalem, beyond the sacred portion (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.23-Ezek.48.28">Eze 48:23-28</reference>). Where was land to be found for them there? A breadth of but four or five miles apiece would be left. As the boundaries of the land are given the same as under Moses, these incongruities cannot be explained away by supposing physical changes about to be effected in the land such as will meet the difficulties of the purely literal interpretation. The distribution of the land is in equal portions among the twelve tribes, without respect to their relative numbers, and the parallel sections running from east to west. There is a difficulty also in the supposed separate existence of the twelve tribes, such separate tribeships no longer existing, and it being hard to imagine how they could be restored as distinct tribes, mingled as they now are. So the stream that issued from the east threshold of the temple and flowed into the Dead Sea, in the rapidity of its increase and the quality of its waters, is unlike anything ever known in Judea or elsewhere in the world. Lastly, the catholicity of the Christian dispensation, and the spirituality of its worship, seem incompatible with a return to the local narrowness and "beggarly elements" of the Jewish ritual and carnal ordinances, disannulled "because of the unprofitableness thereof" [Fairbairn], (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.3">Ga 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">He 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.18">10:18</reference>). "A temple with sacrifices now would be a denial of the all-sufficiency of the sacrifice of Christ. He who sacrificed before confessed the Messiah. He who should sacrifice now would solemnly deny Him" [Douglas]. These difficulties, however, may be all seeming, not real. Faith accepts God's Word as it is, waits for the event, sure that it will clear up all such difficulties. Perhaps, as some think, the beau ideal of a sacred commonwealth is given according to the then existing pattern of temple services, which would be the imagery most familiar to the prophet and his hearers at the time. The minute particularizing of details is in accordance with Ezekiel's style, even in describing purely ideal scenes. The old temple embodied in visible forms and rites spiritual truths affecting the people even when absent from it. So this ideal temple is made in the absence of the outward temple to serve by description the same purpose of symbolical instruction as the old literal temple did by forms and acts. As in the beginning God promised to be a "sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.16">Eze 11:16</reference>) to the captives at the Chebar, so now at the close is promised a complete restoration and realization of the theocratic worship and polity under Messiah in its noblest ideal (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38-Jer.31.40">Jr 31:38-40</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Re 21:22</reference> "no temple" is seen, as in the perfection of the new dispensation the accidents of place and form are no longer needed to realize to Christians what Ezekiel imparts to Jewish minds by the imagery familiar to them. In Ezekiel's temple holiness stretches over the entire temple, so that in this there is no longer a distinction between the different parts, as in the old temple: parts left undeterminate in the latter obtain now a divine sanction, so that all arbitrariness is excluded. So that it is be a perfect manifestation of the love of God to His covenant-people (Eze 40:1-43:12); and from it, as from a new center of religious life, there gushes forth the fulness of blessings to them, and so to all people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:1-23</reference>) [Fairbairn and Havernick]. The temple built at the return from Babylon can only very partially have realized the model here given. The law is seemingly opposed to the gospel (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.21">Mt 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.27">22, 27</reference>, 28, 33, 34). It is not really so (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17">Mt 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.31">Ro 3:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Ga 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.22">22</reference>). It is true Christ's sacrifice superseded the law sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.12-Heb.10.18">He 10:12-18</reference>). Israel's province may hereafter be to show the essential identity, even in the minute details of the temple sacrifices, between the law and gospel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Ro 10:8</reference>). The ideal of the theocratic temple will then first be realized.<div eID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11808"/><hi type="bold">1. beginning of the year--</hi>the ecclesiastical year, the first month of which was Nisan.<div eID="gen21371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city ... thither--</hi>Jerusalem, the center to which all the prophet's thoughts tended. <div eID="gen21372" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11809"/><div sID="gen21373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11809"/><hi type="bold">2. visions of God--</hi>divinely sent visions.<div eID="gen21373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">very high mountain--</hi>Moriah, very high, as compared with the plains of Babylon, still more so as to its moral elevation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">Eze 17:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.40">20:40</reference>).<div eID="gen21374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by which--</hi>Ezekiel coming from the north is set down at (as the Hebrew for "upon" may be translated) Mount Moriah, and sees the city-like frame of the temple stretching southward. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>, "God brings him thither," that is, close up to it, so as to inspect it minutely (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Re 21:10</reference>). In this closing vision, as in the opening one of the book, the divine hand is laid on the prophet, and he is borne away in the visions of God. But the scene there was by the Chebar, Jehovah having forsaken Jerusalem; now it is the mountain of God, Jehovah having returned thither; there, the vision was calculated to inspire terror; here, hope and assurance. <div eID="gen21375" type="x-p"/>

Measures were mostly taken from the human body. The greater cubit, the length from the elbow to the end of the middle finger, a little more than two feet: exceeding the ordinary cubit (from the elbow to the wrist) by an hand-breadth, that is, twenty-one inches in all. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13">Eze 43:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">Eze 40:5</reference>. The palm was the full breadth of the hand, three and a half inches.<div eID="gen21380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breadth of the building--</hi>that is, the boundary wall. The imperfections in the old temple's boundary wall were to have no place here. The buildings attached to it had been sometimes turned to common uses; for example, Jeremiah was imprisoned in one (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">Jr 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">29:26</reference>). But now all these were to be holy to the Lord. The gates and doorways to the city of God were to be imprinted in their architecture with the idea of the exclusion of everything defiled (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Re 21:27</reference>). The east gate was to be especially sacred, as it was through it the glory of God had departed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:23</reference>), and through it the glory was to return (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1">Eze 43:1</reference>, 2; 44:2, 3). <div eID="gen21381" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11818"/><div sID="gen21392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11818"/>18. The higher pavement was level with the entrance of the gates, the lower was on either side of the raised pavement thus formed. Whereas Solomon's temple had an outer court open to alterations and even idolatrous innovations (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.5">1Ch 20:5</reference>), in this there was to be no room for human corruptions. Its compass was exactly defined, one hundred cubits; and the fine pavement implied it was to be trodden only by clean feet (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Is 35:8</reference>). <div eID="gen21392" type="x-p"/>

This court was one hundred cubits square, and had the altar in it, in front of the temple. It was the court of the priests, and hence is connected with those who had charge of the altar and the music. The description here is brief, as the things connected with this portion were from the first divinely regulated. <div eID="gen21407" type="x-p"/>
